checks.claim: each entry carries an arXiv id, DOI or URL a reader can follow
checks.note: an entry nobody can look up cannot support a claim

checks.claim: one paper appears under one id
checks.note: duplicates inflate the apparent breadth of the literature base and split citations of one paper

checks.claim: entries from different years do not share an identifier
checks.note: a shared TITLE splits one paper's citations, which is untidy; a shared IDENTIFIER between works of different years sends the reader to the wrong document, which breaks the citation. This check exists because the title check flagged the PDG and CODATA groups while missing berger1966 carrying Berger 1955's DOI and penrose_2004_road_to_reality carrying a 1996 identifier. Note the blind spot it keeps: an identifier that is simply wrong, and shared with nothing, passes

checks.claim: no two entries share a title once subtitles are dropped
checks.note: Advisory, not a gate. A looser title key would wrongly collapse the deliberate PDG per-section citations, the distinct CODATA releases and two different Acharya papers, so these are surfaced for a human decision rather than merged. This tier is what exposed two books whose DOIs resolved to a DNA nanopore experiment and a magazine price list -- unique identifiers pointing at the wrong document, which no other check can detect

checks.claim: each entry is cited by a formula, section or parameter
checks.note: source_simulation records which module registered an entry -- that is provenance, not citation; it does not say which claim the paper supports

note: Reports, does not repair. Collapsing duplicate ids is an editorial decision about which id is canonical, and orphan entries may be genuinely relevant background that simply has no citation site yet. Both are surfaced so the choice is deliberate rather than accidental.
duplicate_caveat: Detection is by normalised title, so it cannot distinguish an accidental duplicate from a deliberate one, and it cannot tell two different papers apart once their titles have been abbreviated to the same string. Both errors were present. The seven CODATA 2022 entries (codata2022faraday, codata2022hartree, ...) cited one release for seven different constants, which looked like a defensible convention until the entries were compared: all seven were bibliographically identical, and which constant each supports is recorded by the citing module, not by the id, so they were merged and nothing was lost. Two Super-Kamiokande proton-decay searches eight years apart were NOT merged: there the shared title was itself the defect, and restoring the published titles separated them. The count is a starting point for that judgement, not a verdict.
